Hello every-body! The name is Phantom5613, but since you seem like a good kid you can call me Phantom. I'm a new-comer to the SotM Forums, but I've been playing the game for quite some time now. And I've been loving every minute of gameplay(aside from today, when Miss information wiped the floor of the FV HQ with AZ's face, but I swear that the only reason that happened was because the sun was in my eyes! ...And that a T-Rex was eating the rest of him at the time... -.-6 ).

 

I'm not sure if I'm stepping on anybody's toes or posting a topic that is already on a more popular thread, but I'd like to speculate a bit about the as-of-the-typing-of-this-post unknown(to me) heroes of the future 'Vengeance' expansion in the future. If there IS such a thread out there, then I will gladly shut my trap and go visit it. But, since I haven't seen one in the admitedly short time I've been here I will say my piece here for now.

 

As far as we know right now there are five brand spanking new heroes planned for, as I'll call it until you guys come up with a better idea, 'Veng'. Now we haven't gotten any info on these mysterious do-gooders, but I have a few theories...On three of them at least.

 

The first, which I'm the most confident about, I'll nick-name Schrödinger. This guy may be familiar to you, especially if you've played against Kismet or paid attention to the art on Expatriette's Shock Rounds. He's a shaggy hiared guy dressed in a black and yellow spandex suit with a white box chest symbol(Familiar? Here's a hint: Kismet's Nemesis Symbol...) and wears a TMNT style bandana mask. From what I've seen of this guy he has some crappy luck. Not only is he getting his fanny kicked on a few of Kismet's cards, but he's also getting zapped by a (supposed) ally's attack. Now, all that could just be a result of the poor guy being the Trickster's sworn ememy, but I'd like to think that he's just naturally unlucky. None of his powers seem to be too apparent on any of the cards we've seen so far, so I don't really know anything else about him.

 

I'll leave it at that for now. I still need to brew over the other theories of mine...

My next theory comes from yet more card artwork. Specifically "Projected Paralysis" from the Dreamer's deck. Warrning, this is just a theory from a guy with too much free time on his hands...

 

On this card we see the Dreamer restricting a gigantic woman merely with the power of her mind. Now this is really cool, but after looking at her for a moment, something hit me(which was probably obvious to most of you, but I digress). This person has an amazing likeness to another character. Namely the self-made conqueror of the Multiverse, Grand Warlord Voss. Or at the very least she's a Thorathian. The reddish skin, the bony spikes coming from her back and elbows, the glowing eyes...

 

This just got my brain thinking "Okay, this is a Thorathian. But why is she here? Why would she be 'fighting' against the Dreamer?" The alure of even more powerful psychic abbilities that he could control and replicate could be a large draw for someone like Voss, but to me that just doesn't seem his style to send just one person after the Dreamer. She's incredibly powerful and would most-likely take down all but the best of troops, and I think Voss is smart enough to even then not send just one. This leads me to believe that she's a heroine.

 

Now this is just pure speculation on my part but I think that there's a small, teeny-tiny, just about feasable chance that this girl could be the estranged daughter of Voss, or at least related to him. She resembles him more than to the other Thorathians that we've seen(Field Lieutenant Tamar and First Lieutenant Vyktor from Voss' deck and Vicious Cyclone from Temest's, though granted that one seems to also be Vyktor.) with their bluish skin. She seems to have powers not natural to her species which we've only really seen on Voss. Granted we havent's seen Voss grow to giant level heights, but I'm talking about the sheer presence of powers.

 

Or I could be reading into it too much. There's bound to be at least a few Thorathians who didn't whole-heartedly agree with Voss systematically taking over their planet, even if he was a noble.

Each of the expansions has been about a central theme.  Rook city was the dark/gritty expansion.  Relics was about magic and the mystical side of things.  Shattered timelines was about the darkest futures, and how they could happen.

 

What is Vengeance going to be about?  While on the surface its about a villain team, and the moment for the villains to take front stage, I'm thinking that the root theme is change.

 

At a gameplay level it defines a new way of playing the game.  It is a standalone type of game, as opposed to the standard expansion.  Plotwise, I suspect we're going to see some major, major changes for the heroes.  This may well be when we see which Legacy survives.

In terms of the heroes, I think that they are going to be extensions of that theme.  We're going to see heroes who fit with the theme of change.  So- heroes who used to be villains, heroes who are radically different mechanically, or heroes who hint at entirely new sides/agendas in the sentinels conflict.

 

Con may well fit that description, but something tells me that we're going to see a very science/tech heavy expansion soon.  I'm guessing thats when we'll finally see Unity and AZ's individual nemeses (I'm counting the V5 as a group nemesis).  If Con is an AI, or (as some have suggested) a future AI fusion of Unity/Fixer, then the superscience time is when to let it step up and make a grand entrance. * An Oracle-type hacker/info specialist who supports the heroes without being a target.  (This would require special rules printed on the card which aren't a Power, and that would be unprecedented, but I wouldn't be surprised if that happens with The Sentinels anyway.

Except that the point of the Lovecraftiverse is that no amount of power is ever enough.  Indeed, pretty much Lovecraft's entire concept was that the more science learns about the world, the more hopeless humanity's place in the world becomes - which is at best questionably true for other reasons, but the whole reason he invented Cthulhu was to personify his feelings on the topic, and so Cthulhu represents the ultimate "shut up you're wrong" to any arguments against the original premise he's connected to, which was in large part that there are some fights you can't possibly win, riddles you can't solve and would be happier not trying to.  Superman, in particular (being the original and archetypal superhero, and the invention of a couple of Jewish kids who needed a symbol of hopefulness to escape the troubles of their lives), is likewise a "shut up you're wrong" in favor of a different premise - he brings godlike, unstoppable power to the cause of Truth, Justice and the American Way, while Cthulhu brings ultimate, inescapable horror to the cause of Humanity is Doomed And Nothing Can Save Us.  If you disagree with either of those premises, that's perfectly fine, it just means you really shouldn't use the character who exists only to prove them right (or other very similar characters, and there's no way Ixthulhu's name is a coincidence…if you want a horrible-but-ultimately-beatable alien god-thing, you shouldn't try to conflate him with an unbeatable one).

You can't say that mixing the two mythos don't work when the story produced by it is actually entertaining and fun to watch.

I can and do say exactly that (with the understanding that I am speaking from partial ignorance, and might change my mind upon actually watching the whole thing).  Sometimes, the point of a story is not just to be entertaining and fun to watch (indeed, many of the greatest and most beloved stories are utterly gut-wrenching tragedies and rage-inducers…Romeo & Juliet and A Game of Thrones spring to mind offhand).  Sometimes, it exists to deliver an Aesop, and anything which breaks the Aesop can utterly destroy the raison d'etre of the story…or, in this case, a story element which was used in a story where it didn't belong.

That's like saying you can't make a good comedy with zombies because the existence of zombies is diametrically opposite to the tone of a comedy, and putting them in a comedy is a huge mistreatment of them. Both Fido and Shawn of the Dead are fantastic movies. The zombies are the same as they've always been in both of those movies, but the protagonists treat them differently. It's a different kind of story than what those characters are normally in, but simply changing genres does not invalidate or ruin a character. It just shows them in a different light.

Sometimes, showing something in a different light exposes hideous flaws which scar all perceptions of its worth altogether.  This is the entire reason that fashion photos are airbrushed…one unflattering image becomes a blight upon the career of someone who was once valued for their apparent flawlessness.  If you turn Cthulhu into a laughingstock, then people who encounter him first as a laughingstock will never appreciate what he should be.  If someone wrote a Superman story in which he chain-smoked and beat his wife, DC Comics would sue the pants off that person, because they aren't just using DC's "intellectual property" without permission, but horribly misusing it, in a way that irreparably damages their brand…people would see that story and think that was the "real" Superman.  Unfortunately, nobody owns Cthulhu, and thus nobody can stop writers from abusing Cthulhu in exactly such a fashion.  (I think IP law is an imperfect solution at best for preventing such mis-representations of characters, but it's the one we have at the moment.)

In conclusion, if Cthulhu (or his thinly-disguised pastiche) is to appear in a superhero story at all, I want him to be treated with the gravity he deserves.  Consider the way X-Men comics handled the Legacy Virus…it was a metaphor for AIDS, and because AIDS hadn't been cured, the writers weren't allowed to cure it, but had to write about how the heroes handled the fact that they were victims of something they couldn't win against.  That's what you use Cthulhu for - to show how your characters deal with loss, futility, and ultimate doom.  Whether superheroes ever should accept the inevitability of their defeat, when doing exactly the opposite is pretty much their raison d'etre, is another question (and I don't think it's a coincidence that Marvel, not DC, did the Legacy Virus).  But that brings me right back to my "Cthulhu should probably not be in superheroes" premise.

My one thing with Akash is that she's the one villain I basically refuse to play non-Advanced.  Even Ambuscade has managed to kick my butt on Regular once, and certainly there are reasons to not want to put up with the nuisance his advanced version presents, ditto for Omnitron...both are wimps without advanced text, but sometimes I'm in the mood to beat up on a wimp.  Thing is, Abby is not that much harder on Advanced (if you're going to beat up a 200-HP mountain anyway, what difference does it make if it takes a little longer due to damage reduction, or if she hits back every turn in the late game).  But without the Advanced mode's offense/defense switch, there just isn't much difference between the two sides.  Pre-flip, she gets extra plays for every Environment target played, while post-flip she only gets them when said targets die.  That and a little durdling with the Environment deck are the only differences apart from the advanced text, and it makes me feel as if bothering to track her flip mechanic is a pointless waste of time.  Thusly, I only ever want to fight her on Advanced, since that way you instantly know when she's flipped, and it makes a huge difference.

(I suppose in this regard she's the exact opposite of Gloomweaver.  Nobody fails to notice when he flips, but the difference between his regular and advanced modes pre-flip is irrelevant to his nemesis and a good many other heroes.  This is the chief reason why I'd want a promo Gloomweaver - not because he's too weak, but just because he doesn't really feel like a proper Call of Cthulhu villain to me, in that he functions too much like an "average" villain, when his concept ought to make him a particularly special snowflake.)

Her difficulty has always been more dependant on the environment than normal/advanced mode text. 

Normal mode, her flip side is not supposed to be "harder" per say (I think thats an easy assumption to fall into for villains. Its not the case). What it does accomplish is to change the situation up and force a different perspective. There is a much different level on control on either side, and while nuanced it may be, it is far from pointless. 

Advanced mode turns up the heat on the flip side with extra unscaled damage (always scary to see in low [H] games) and the innate DR for villain targets on the front side serves the purpose of slowing her death just enough to try and squeak out flipping more than once per. 

There are reasons why it was designed the way it was. By dissmissing those things and calling them "pointless", you'll miss the greater picture of what the effects are trying to accomplish.

A new year, a new conspiracy theory.

Ever since I saw the promo for GI Bunker, I've been wondering who was in that suit.  See- I have this theory that the fates of the Bunker pilots are intertwined, and I think that each of the pilots are funhouse reflections of one another.

First- we have the upstanding Tyler Vance.  He's the very definition of heroic. He's honest, upstanding, heart of gold, keeps going no matter the odds, and makes the ultimate sacrifice (in Iron Legacy's timeline) to fight evil.  

Second, we have Stephen graves- the envious rival who becomes more and more twisted and grotesque as his jealousy (and consumption of chemical enhancements) grows.  Despite this, he eventually reforms and becomes a hero when the person he was competing with dies fighting evil.  

Basically, we have two patterns that are in play- the hero and the reformed villain .  And here's where it gets interesting. 

Who is GI Bunker?

I don't think that its a random person.  I think that we've already met the pilot.  I think....its Chairman Pike.  

We know that Pike is old enough to have fought in the war and he's got distinctive facial characteristics (rockin' the stache) that would make him immediately recognizable even in a 1940's military uniform (or a scientist coat, or the wrecked GI armor).

AND- if it was pike, it would fit with the character pattern established by Tyler and graves.

Tyler is the Hero, Graves is the Reformed Villain, Pike is the Fallen Hero.  It adds a whole new element to his story, and even provides some interesting new angles.  Maybe he started the organization as a way to tame the rampant Crime in Rook city, and (over time) became what he was trying to prevent?  Maybe he's always had a rotten core, even when trying to be a hero. Maybe he was crippled in the GI suit, and thats why he began his life extension/body rejuvenation experiments in the first place.

But wait- theres more!

If Pike is the GI suit pilot (maybe even the original DESIGNER of the suit), that opens up an entirely new can of worms for future plot developments.  

Picture this... Pike has been intrinsic to the development of the Bunker project from day 1.  He comes home from the war a hero, and proceeds to build an empire.  Naturally, when the government decides to continue the project, they ask for his input.  Maybe he doesn't take part directly...but he is in the loop the entire time.  

When the government needs specialty parts, you can bet that Pike industries is in the running for that contract!  

What if Bunker's future holds the terrifying revelation that all of his armor has been built and modified- for years- by one of the F5's greatest foes?

What if that foe (who knows EXACTLY how to operate those suits) rigs them for remote operation (using loyal agents, or unwitting pawns)? It could be done under the guise of a legitimate upgrade- since we know that the Bunker suits are in a constant cycle of maintenance and development, and there is a large support crew.

It would complete the plot circle of heroes turning into villains and villains turning into heroes- you have the pilot who always made the right choice being perceived as a villain, and having to fight against his own suits.  

Bunker vs. the Hall of Armor!

right now, AZ's story is at a virtual standstill.  we need a crisis that affects him personally to really see him step up and accept his heroic status.  for his story to pregoress, he needs to make a mistake and then (instead of running or getting depressed) step up and do something to fix it.

I finally got to play sentinels with other people, and when trying to explain some things to them I had a few thoughts. They also inspired me to do some heavy duty looking into so I might be posting here a bit in the coming weeks if I find something interesting.

 

1st: Less likely now that I did a little research, but still possible. Mainstay and Medico's developing powers seems a tad bit random. Not only is there very little in the explanation of why they slowly developed powers, but the nature of them and where it all happened are a bit shadowy as well. Plus we don't know who else mught have been effected. We do know it happened in college, we do know that it happened some years before (Medico goes through med school which happens after the general college where he and mainstay were changed).... woah... let's say medico did 4 years pre-med while in college with Mainstay. Then 4 years med school, that means that before they met Idealist it is safe to say they were exposed for approx. 8 years. How old is Idealist when her developing powers and her scientist mother's crazy cause issues? 8 years old. Mainstay and Medico's known locations are Wintersburg Arizona and Pheonix Arizona, which are only a very few miles apart, so it is possible that the college is very close to Pheonix, where Idealist was born and her mother was a scientist working with energy related to Medico. So it is possible that whatever gave Medico and Mainstay powers could have also given Idealist her powers.

My oringal point? Mainstay, Medico and Idealist might have gained powers from one of those myterious crystals that we see in Tactics and that we know gave Cosmic and Infinitor powers. If the crystal were being experimented on by the college it would be possible that the radiation could be diluted so that the power's were gradual. Also, Medico and Cosmic do use the same color energy and Medico could be considered an energy construct. One big hole in the theory is that Medico and Mainstay are listed with "Nuclear Radiation" as a power source, while Idealist is Unknown. The wiki says Idealists flip side references Houe of M and reality shifting powers so it is still possible to some extent.

 

Tangent: I wonder if Idealist's mother is a villain? She's never named, which is suspicious. Knocking her thru the wall might not have killed her (especaly with a device meant to change reality to bring her dead husband back to life) but instead might have left her wheelchair bound (the lady from the Crackjaw Crew?) or something similiar.

 

2nd tangent: Glimpsed at the tactics bios for the citizens, a few might have gotten their powers in similiar ways maybe even from the same source, but something else caught my eye. Truth and Dare came from project Cocoon, but Visionary (AKA Dreamer) was supposedly the only successfully born super from that project. Also Truth and Dare are decades older than the Dreamer. Finally, we have no idea who or what is actually behind Coccoon. It was supposedly the U.S. Government, but they weren't greenlit by the gov't until well after Truth and Dare were born and escaped. Secretary of Defense Anthony Partin supposedly set up Coccoon according to Visionary's bio, but none of that should have happened yet in the Sentinels Timeline. Very Strange disconnect there

What if Fanatic is the "child" in the center? I doubt it, but there are some things we don't know that are interesting.

 

For example: Why did Fanatic come back to life. She would believe the Hand of God, but God works mysteriously and usually thru a third party. We also have a second person we know who was killed and came back to life, Haka. Interestingly it is possible to draw a lot of comparisons between Fanatic's power and Haka's, most importantly that they are both fueled by tradition and belief. Haka in his Ancient Maori chants and practices, Fanatic thru Christianity. What if they can be traced back to an original source? What if Haka was a sort of first test, the next we know of being Fanatic.

 

It might be possible to say Fanatic's ressurection was a one-time thing, while we know Haka is effectively immortal (holy crap, Haka is a hero version of Vandal Savage, I just got that!). However, I point you to her armor. It is one of the only cards in the game that can bring a hero back after they've hit 0 or less hp. And we have good reason to suspect that the armor is not inately powerful. Look at her backstory, the armor and sword she found her not that special. However, one morning she awoke, supposedly after using her own blood to write runes on her sword, which had now become Absolution. Where did the Aegis come from? Her armor wasn't carved in runes, but her blood could easily have infused the armor over the course of a few battles, and would therefore come to represent her ability to heal and revive very quickly.

 

Actually, even the Monty Python easter egg comparing her to the black knight could be a clue. The black knight was being spoofed, but he was able to survive any wound dealt to him without dying of blood loss, essentially immortal.
